summary: Registers the application/smil and application/smil+xml media types for versions 1.0, 2.0 and 2.1 of the Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language. SMIL combines separate multimedia objects, such as video, audio and text, into one synchronized presentation. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: SMIL is like a script for a school play that says when the music starts, when the picture appears and when the words show up. This memo gives that script file its official name tag.

subtitle: Official MIME types for synchronized multimedia presentations.

tldr.problem: The Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL) files have no registered MIME types, so browsers and servers do not know how to handle them or which player to use.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4536 registers two MIME types: application/smil (for SMIL documents) and application/smil+xml (for XML-based SMIL), covering versions 1.0, 2.0 and 2.1 of the specification.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now send SMIL files with the correct content type, and SMIL players can be registered in the operating system to open these files. The registration enables content negotiation between SMIL-aware and non-SMIL-aware clients.

today: RFC 4536 is informational and registers the SMIL media types with IANA. The application/smil type is marked OBSOLETE, while application/smil+xml is marked COMMON for ongoing use with SMIL 2.0, 2.1, and future versions.

sections.title: What SMIL Is
sections.content:
The Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL) is a language, defined by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), that combines separate multimedia objects—such as video, audio, images, and text—into a single synchronized presentation. A SMIL document describes when each piece plays, how it is positioned on the screen, what hyperlinks attach to it, and which pieces to include or exclude based on system capabilities.

RFC 4536 registers official MIME media types for SMIL versions 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1, so that servers, browsers, and players can correctly identify and handle SMIL files.
sections.eli5: SMIL files are scripts that say: play this video here, then show this picture there, and at the same time play this audio. Instead of a person directing the play, a computer reads the SMIL script and makes it happen.

sections.title: Registered MIME Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers two MIME types:

  • application/smil is marked as OBSOLETE and covers SMIL 1.0 and 2.0.
  • application/smil+xml is marked as COMMON and covers SMIL 2.0, 2.1, and newer versions that use XML syntax.

Both types use the same optional parameters: charset (for character encoding) and profile (a URI identifying a specific SMIL dialect or profile). The profile parameter is intended for content negotiation, such as in HTTP Accept headers, to negotiate support for SMIL Basic (a subset of SMIL 2.0).
sections.eli5: SMIL files get two official file-type names. One is old (for SMIL 1.0 and 2.0), and one is current (for newer versions). Both can optionally say what encoding they use and what features they need.

sections.title: File Format and Recognition
sections.content:
SMIL files are XML documents, so they start with optional XML declarations and contain SMIL elements. All SMIL files begin with the string <smil near the start. SMIL 2.0 and 2.1 files declare a namespace URL (for example, xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2001/SMIL20/Language'), which helps identify which version of SMIL the file uses.

Common file extensions are .smil, .smi (though this collides with other formats on Windows and Mac), and .sml. On Macintosh systems, file type codes include 'TEXT', 'SMIL', and '.SMI'.
sections.eli5: SMIL files are text that starts with <smil and looks like HTML but with special rules. They can have different file endings (.smil, .smi, .sml) and the computer recognizes them by looking inside.

sections.title: The Profile Parameter
sections.content:
The optional 'profile' parameter lets clients and proxies negotiate which SMIL features are needed. A SMIL player that only supports SMIL Basic (a simplified subset of SMIL 2.0) can advertise this in an HTTP Accept header, for example: 'Accept: application/smil+xml; profile="http://www.w3.org/2001/SMIL20/HostLanguage"'. Proxies and transcoders can use this to decide whether to deliver or transcode a SMIL document.

This parameter is inspired by the same mechanism in the application/xhtml+xml media type and is intended for use during content negotiation, not for delivery. Origin servers are not required to understand or use it.
sections.eli5: The profile parameter is like saying 'I can only play basic SMIL, not the fancy version.' Servers and proxies can use this to send you a simpler version if you ask for it.

sections.title: Security Risks in SMIL
sections.content:
SMIL documents can define infinite loops, which is necessary for multimedia playback but allows a malicious author to create content that plays forever. SMIL players should provide a stop button or other controls so users can interrupt playback.

SMIL documents link to other media (images, sounds, videos, text). These links are typically followed automatically by SMIL players, so a malicious document can cause unwanted downloads without explicit user consent. Each linked media file carries its own security risks.

SMIL 'switch' elements can contain different alternatives for different players or systems. A switch does not guarantee that all alternatives present the same information, so a malicious author can show different content to different viewers while claiming to show the same thing.

Beyond these SMIL-specific concerns, all security considerations of RFC 3023 (XML Media Types) apply.
sections.eli5: SMIL can cause problems if someone makes a file that loops forever, automatically downloads lots of stuff, or tricks different players into showing different pictures. SMIL players need safeguards, and users should be careful where they get SMIL files from.
